messages.content: if i say i would like to visit tomorrow, is that the same as saying i will visit tomorrow?
would like gives what you want. will visit sounds like a plan. you can want a visit before knowing whether it works for the other person.
say it simply.
would like says what you want. will visit says it more like something you have chosen to do.
write a kind message to my aunt asking about tomorrow without choosing for her.
i would like to visit tomorrow. would that be a good day for you?
she says she wants to see me but is not sure about tomorrow yet.
then the wish to meet is clear, but the day is still open. you can give her time: that is okay. tell me when you know, and we can choose a time together.
does her not knowing the day mean she does not want the visit?
no. she said she wants to see you. she can want a visit and not know which day works yet.
answer simply.
no. she wants a visit, but she does not know if tomorrow works.
what if i need to choose today because of a train?
then tell her that detail so she knows why you need an answer: i need to choose my train today. would another day be better if tomorrow is not clear yet?
tell me a story about a teacher reading the wrong line and a child helping her find the right one. do not make the teacher know everything.

a teacher reads a book while a child looks at the same page. the teacher leaves out a line. the child asks whether they should read that part too. the teacher stops and looks back. she sees the line she left out and thanks the child for asking. they read it together and understand the next part better. the child learns that asking a question can help everyone, even the person doing the teaching.
make it simple.
a teacher reads a book while a child looks at the same page. she leaves out a line. the child asks about it, and she looks back. they read the line together and understand the next part better.
was the child wrong to ask just because a teacher was reading?
no. the question was about something the child could see on the page. a useful question can help them read the whole part together.
say it simply.
no. the child saw a line that was not read. asking helped them read the whole part together.
write what the teacher could say.
thank you for asking. i left out that line. let us read it before going on.
does that say every teacher always leaves out lines?
no. it is one thing that happened in a made up story, rather than a rule about all teaching.
three people eat at one table. one has soup, one has rice, and one has bread and cheese. can we say they had the same meal?
they ate together, but each chose different food. that keeps both ideas clear.
answer simply.
they had time together at a table, but did not eat the same food.
write a short conversation where they choose a drink they all want.
would everyone like tea? yes, i would. so would i. i would too. then we can ask for three cups of tea.
does having tea together change the food each person had?
no. they can have the same drink with different food. you should not change the soup, rice, or bread and cheese just because all three chose tea.
now one person wants water instead. how many cups of tea should they ask for?
two cups of tea and one cup of water, if the other two still want tea.
can there still be three people while one choice changes?
yes. changing one drink does not change the number of people. there are still three people and three drinks in this example.
answer simply.
yes. the same three people can change what one of them wants to drink.
my computer is on. does that mean i am working right now?
no. a computer can be on for music, a game, writing, or another use. you would need more information to know what you are doing.
what if the screen has a page of writing?
that gives more information about the screen, but not for sure what the person is doing. they could have left the page there while doing something else.
answer simply.
it gives a detail about the screen. it still does not say what the person is doing now.
write a small story with a person leaving work open while talking to a friend.

a woman has a page of work on her computer. her friend comes in, and she stops writing to talk. the screen still has the page on it. later, her brother sees it and asks whether she is working. she says no, she is talking now and will return to the page later.
does the page still being on the screen make her answer false?
no. the page can be on the screen while she is talking instead of writing.
answer simply.
no. the screen does not tell us everything about what she is doing.
what question would help rather than choosing from the screen alone?
are you working now, or is that page just still open?
i saw someone working in a garden. can i know that every plant there is theirs?
not from that alone. they could own it, help a friend, or work with a group. doing work in a place does not always tell you whose place it is.
write a simple question to ask without saying i already know.
is this your garden, or are you helping someone with it?
they say it is a garden used by a group, and they look after one part.
then you know something more specific: they do work in one part of a garden used by a group. that does not make every plant theirs alone.
can you write a short story with that detail?

a child sees a person working near some vegetables in a garden. she asks whether all the plants are his. he says that the garden is for a group and this is the part he helps with. he says someone else helps with the flowers in another area. she asks whether the group chooses new plants together.
change only the sentence about the flowers.
he says someone else helps with the flowers in another area.
does saying the garden is for a group tell us how many people are in it?
no. group is general. you would need another detail for the number of people.
write that question.
how many people work in the garden group?
i came home before lunch, but after my sister made soup. does that give an order for three things?
yes. your sister made soup first. you came home after that. lunch came after you got home. that is the order from your sentence.
does it tell us how many minutes were between them?
no. before and after give order, rather than a number of minutes. the things could be close together or far apart in time.
say my question simply.
does it tell us how many minutes were between them?
write a short story with that order and no new time.
my sister made soup before i came home. after i got home, we had lunch.
keep the story to two sentences.
my sister made soup before i came home. after i got home, we had lunch.
can i change after i got home to before i got home without changing the meaning?
no. that would put lunch before your return, which is a different order. moving one time word can change the story.
what is the order in simple words?
soup made, then home, then lunch.
give it as a short full sentence.
my sister made soup, i came home, and then we had lunch.
my friend asks me to explain a question, not give the answer. how can i help?
you can ask which part is not clear and use a different small example. then let your friend try the original question after understanding the idea.
the question is two cups and three more, but i want an example with another number.
you could show one cup and two more, then ask how many there are. after that, your friend can use the same way of thinking for two and three.
say my last request simply.
the question is two cups and three more. give an example with a different number.
can i ask what they think first?
yes. asking how they started can help you see whether the problem is the words, the number, or the next thing to do.
write that question.
what have you tried, and which part is not clear yet?
does helping mean i must do the whole task for them?
no. help can be a question, a small example, or one part made clear. your friend can still work out the answer.
answer simply.
no. you can help with one part and let your friend work out the answer.
write a quiet story where a child can hear music in a house but finds different people in different rooms. use three people and no more.

a child sits in her room and can hear music. she goes to the living room and finds her mother reading. her mother says the music is from the kitchen. there, her grandfather is making tea with the radio on. the child asks if they can all sit together for one song. the mother brings her book, the grandfather brings the tea, and the three sit near the table. when the song is over, each chooses what to do next.
ask my request simply.
write a quiet story where a child can hear music and finds her mother and grandfather in different rooms.
who made the music in the story?
the music came from the radio. the grandfather had it on, but he was making tea rather than making the song.
answer simply.
the radio gave the music. the grandfather had it on, but he was making tea rather than making the song.
where were all three at the end of the song?
near the table together. the story does not say which room that table is in, so we should not choose that detail for sure.
can you add that it was the kitchen table?
yes. they all sit near the kitchen table until the song is over.
did adding the room change the number of people?
no. it is still the child, her mother, and her grandfather.
i want to ask my cousin if they want to visit again. i enjoyed the last visit, but they have not said whether they did.
you can speak for yourself and ask about their choice: i enjoyed your last visit. would you like to come again another day?
can you add that i think we both enjoyed the visit?
that would add a feeling for your cousin that you do not know yet. you could ask instead: did you enjoy the visit too?
say my last request simply.
add that i think we both enjoyed the visit.
now write the message without making up their feeling.
i enjoyed your last visit. did you enjoy it too? i would like to see you again if you would like another visit.
what if they answer only the question about how they felt during the visit?
then you know how they felt about the last visit, but not whether or when they want another one. you can ask about a new visit too if that is important.
answer simply.
the old visit and a new visit are different questions. if they liked the old visit, you still need to ask about another day.
say it simply.
they can like the old visit without having chosen a new one.
can adding a few words to a request help a conversation even if the sentence gets longer?

yes. a few useful words can help the other person know what you mean without asking again. bring the book may need more context, while bring the blue book from my desk gives a specific object and place.
explain simply.
a few useful words can help the other person know what you mean without asking again.
what if there are two blue books on the desk?
then color and place are still not enough to choose one. add another real detail, such as what the book is about, or ask the person to check with you.
write a request for the blue book about a village.
please bring the blue book about a village from my desk.
does more detail always make the request more correct?
no. details must come from what you know. a long request with made up details can send someone to the wrong object.
say it simply.
a made up detail can make someone choose the wrong object. use real details, rather than add words just to sound sure.
what if i do not know which blue book it is?
say that and ask for help looking. you can say you do not know which one, then ask to look together.
answer simply.
you can say you do not know which one, then ask to look together.
i gave a drawing to my friend to look at, then they thought they could keep it. how can i make what i wanted clear?
you could say: i wanted you to look at it, not keep it. could i have it back, please?
use wanted in the request.
i wanted you to look at it, not keep it. could i have it back, please?
can that be kind without saying they did something wrong?
yes. you can ask for it back without choosing a reason for what happened. the words may not have been clear before.
answer simply.
yes. the words may not have been clear before. you can make the request clear now.
give only the request.
could i have the drawing back, please? i wanted you to look at it for a while.
what can i say if i do want them to keep another drawing?
you can make that choice clear: this other drawing is for you to keep.
does another mean the first drawing has changed?
no. another is a different drawing. the first one can still be returned.
answer simply.
another is a different drawing. the first one can still be returned.
picoboi, answer my next question with one word. is four more than three?
yes.
now answer in a full sentence. did you need to explain more before?
no. you asked for one word, and yes gave the right answer to that question.
answer simply.
no. yes gave the right answer in the short way you asked for.
now tell me whether i have four books at home.
i do not know how many books you have at home unless you tell me.
if i ask for one word there, should you just say yes?
no. asking for one word does not tell me how many books you have. i should say i do not know rather than give a false yes or no.
answer simply.
no. asking for one word does not tell me how many books you have. i should say i do not know.
what if i tell you i have four and ask whether it is more than three?
then yes is a right short answer using the information you gave.
can you ask one question to learn the number instead of choosing it without information?
how many books do you have at home?
say my request simply.
ask how many books i have before choosing an answer.
